keyFindings.description: The new skip in settleEndedHolds' failed-restore loop tests the topic alone - `if (topic === claimedRoleTopic) continue;` - while its comment claims the matching topic means 'a newer move's claim, which dropped every hand-back of it left pending'. That is not guaranteed: claimedRoleTopic is also set, a few lines above in this same loop, by the unconfirmed adoption at :2281-2285, which writes claimedRoleTopic = hold.topic, claimedRoleSessionID = hold.id and holdUnconfirmed = true without the listener having confirmed anything. So when pendingHandBacks carries two entries of one topic under different sessions - reachable because setEnvoyRole's abandoned branch adds `<topic>@<id>` at :1929 without the dedupe delete that only a live, claimed branch performs at :1938-1941 - the loop adopts the wanted one and then drops the other instead of recording abandonedHolds[topic] = {the other session}. The lost record is exactly what observeAbandonedHold reads (:1864-1865) to tell this process's own stale holder, which the listener will reap, from a genuine competitor: without it the next refusal records refusedRoles[id] = role (:1978), desiredRole then answers undefined for that session (:2036-2039), and the pane stops trying for the role until a session event or an explicit claim clears it - a live pane that should have reclaimed the role once the stale hold expired does not. Round 4's behaviour here was to restore always, whose worst case I audited as a redundant soft claim of a role the session already holds; this round traded that harmless redundancy for a sticky refusal in the harm class. Fix: discriminate on confirmation, not on the topic - `if (topic === claimedRoleTopic && !holdUnconfirmed) continue;`. Not the session id: a confirmed claim legitimately carries a different claimedRoleSessionID from the failed hold's, so `id === claimedRoleSessionID` would restore exactly the case the skip exists for. Reverting the line to round 4's unconditional restore is also acceptable, since that behaviour is audited and bounded.

The header says that at equality 'the third refresh is due at the very instant the record expires', which conflates dispatch with completion. With the suite's own tie fixture (heartbeat 40000, call budget 60000, lifetime 180000) the third refresh is due at 120000 ms and its budgeted completion reaches 180000. The rule is right and the fixtures are right; the sentence explaining them is not, and it is the sentence a future timing change starts from. Say that the third refresh's budgeted completion reaches expiry, leaving no scheduling margin.

roundFourFindingsVerified: check-heartbeat-margin.sh:261 is `renewal_window >= lifetime.value`, with the message naming 'equal to' or 'past' and stating that the tie is refused as surely as what is past it.

The remedy arithmetic moved with the comparison and went further: max_heartbeat = (lifetime - call_budget - 1) // RENEWALS // SECOND * SECOND and min_lifetime = (renewal_window // SECOND + 1) * SECOND, rounded to whole seconds because the Go sites a maintainer edits are parsed as whole seconds or minutes. The suite proves both by applying each prescribed remedy to a complete fixture (exit 0 at 177000 against 180000, and at 180000 against 181000), and refuses the tie itself at exactly 180000.
The subsumed two-interval rule and its worst_case term are gone from the check, its suite and the smoke; the header reads four rules and keeps the backstop paragraph in full under rule 1.
